summary:
My project is called **Ghazal: Mission Engineer**. I created this game because I wanted to make space engineering something that students can enjoy and understand by actually trying it themselves.

In my game, the player becomes a space engineer and chooses one of three missions: tracking dust storms, detecting wildfires, or monitoring floods.

The player starts by exploring NASA satellite images to understand the mission. Then, they design their own satellite by choosing the right equipment, solar panels, batteries, communication systems, orbit, and rocket. They have to think about the budget, weight, and power before launching.

Once the satellite is in space, the player faces different situations and makes decisions to complete the mission and send information back to Earth.

The fun part is that not every mission succeeds on the first try. Players can discover their mistakes, improve their designs, and try again to earn higher scores and badges.

Through this game, I want students to experience how space missions are planned and understand how space technology can help us solve problems on Earth.
details:
Ghazal: Mission Engineer is an interactive game I created to help students experience what it is like to be a space engineer through fun challenges and real decision-making.

How does my game work?

Players choose one of three missions: Desert Shield, Forest Guardian, or Flood Watch. They explore NASA satellite observations, then design their own satellite by choosing seven systems. They must balance the budget, weight, power, and communication before launching. During the mission, they face five challenges, make decisions, and try to collect scientific information and send it back to Earth.

What are the benefits and expected impact?

My goal is to make space engineering easier and more exciting for students. The game encourages problem-solving, critical thinking, and learning from mistakes. It supports Arabic and English and has three difficulty levels.

What tools did I use?

I developed the game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI assistance for coding and illustrations. I also used NASA Earth-observation resources and NASA/JPL orbital information. The mission results are educational simulations.

What challenges did I face?

The hardest part was making the engineering decisions meaningful while keeping the game simple and enjoyable for younger students.

What makes my project creative?

Instead of just learning facts, players build, test, launch, and improve their own satellites. Every decision affects their mission, and they can try again to earn better scores and medals.

What did we consider during development?

We focused on scientific accuracy, clear instructions, attractive visuals, and making sure the satellite's different systems work together.

I hope my game inspires more students to explore space engineering and discover how satellites can help protect Earth.
